newsitem.title: EGYPT: Hope of survivors in Cairo collapse dims - rescuers.
newsitem.headline: Hope of survivors in Cairo collapse dims - rescuers.

text.p: The stench of decomposing corpses enveloped the debris of a collapsed Cairo building as rescue workers raced against time on Wednesday to find any survivors among the 80 or more people feared still buried in the rubble.

At least 31 people were killed when the 11-storey building crumbled into a mountain of dust and twisted metal on Sunday night. More than 24 survivors were dug from the rubble but rescuers say four later died in hospital.
On Tuesday, rescuers pulled out two women alive after 36 hours entombed in the rubble but a German Red Cross worker said chances of finding more survivors were evaporating.
"There might be survivors but chances are getting dimmer and dimmer," Freider Schafer told Reuters. "Normally we say 50 to 60 hours is the absolute maximum time to survive. It's already past that."

Egyptian rescuers, joined by the seven German volunteers, reduced the rubble to a step pyramid of twisted metal, personal belongings and broken bricks. Japanese rescuers were arriving later on Wednesday to help.
Sniffer dogs clambered up and into a central hole dug by rescuers while their handlers wielded equipment to detect any sounds of life.
"On the outside, there are only dead people. There may be a big hole in the centre with living persons," Claus Ropper of the German rescue team said.
Sniffer dogs on Tuesday located American Samantha Miksche, 36 hours after she was entombed with Egyptian friend Noha Fawzi under the collapsed building. Fawzi's aunt and cousin remained missing.
"I just saw the wall in front of us crashing down and then the ceiling was coming down," Miksche, whose mother was still trapped under the rubble, told Reuters.

"The next thing I knew is that I was in a small position, like when the baby is in the mom's stomach, curled up. The ceiling was up to my waist and I couldn't move," the badly-scratched and dazed woman added.
Haggard relatives kept up their vigil at the building site as rescuers removed unbroken crystal glasses, dinnerware and stuffed toys from the debris.
A woman screamed hysterically when rescuers asked the crowd to read the name written on a child's school bag and another rocked and talked to herself, oblivious to her surroundings.

Authorities said the building had been illegally heightened and are questioning the owner. Rescuers said the structure appears to have listed to the left and its porter said he thought renovations in one of its 40 apartments might have destabilised the building.

Officials quoted in the state-owned press promised tougher punishments -- beyond fines -- for unlicensed buildings and parliament is expected to discuss drafting a law banning people from renovating flats without expert permission.

Soaring real estate prices have encouraged landlords to add extra floors illegally. Several buildings have collapsed beneath the extra weight and recent earthquakes have also taken their toll on poorly constructed buildings in the crowded capital.
